title: The Prophet's character
hook: Aisha said his character was the Qur'an (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the renewers who kept walking upstream to the Qur'an and the sunnah. Your line was back to the source.

Tell me about his character. What was he actually like? A man named Sa'd ibn Hisham has come to Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, with a list of things he wants to understand, and this is the big one. He might have expected a story, or a list of virtues. Aisha answers with a question of her own. Don't you read the Qur'an? Yes, he says. Then, she says, his character was the Qur'an. That short exchange is kept in Sahih Muslim.
screen: `TELL ME ABOUT HIS CHARACTER.` → `DON'T YOU READ THE QUR'AN?` → `HIS CHARACTER WAS THE QUR'AN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Arabic it's khuluq: character, disposition, the way a person habitually is. The same word sits in a verse addressed to the Prophet himself, in Pickthall's translation: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." Nature there is khuluq. So Aisha's answer points straight back to the book. Second, what her answer does. She doesn't hand Sa'd a portrait; she hands him a text he already owns. If you want to know the man, read what he lived by: the patience, the honesty, the mercy, the prayer at night. Some readers take her words in two directions at once: the Qur'an shows what his character was, and his life shows what the Qur'an looks like when a person actually does it. Third, the small evidence. The hadith collections keep ordinary moments, not only great ones. Asked what he did at home, Aisha said he kept busy serving his family, and when the call to prayer came he went out to pray. That's in Sahih al-Bukhari. Anas, who served him as a boy for ten years, said he was never once told off with so much as a sigh of annoyance, never asked why did you do that. Bukhari keeps that too. And a saying in Tirmidhi counts a smile at your brother as charity. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary afternoon. A character is built from habits, and habits are small enough to copy. Nobody copies a whole life in a day. But one habit, a smile, a hand with the dishes, holding back the irritated sigh, can be tried before dinner.
screen: `KHULUQ: THE WAY A PERSON HABITUALLY IS.` · `SHE HANDED HIM A BOOK, NOT A PORTRAIT.` · `SMALL MOMENTS: HOME, A SERVANT, A SMILE.` · `HABITS ARE SMALL ENOUGH TO COPY.` · then, large: `AND LO! THOU ART OF A TREMENDOUS NATURE.`

segments.voice: Choose one of his habits: helping at home without being asked, holding back the sigh when someone gets something wrong, or a real smile for someone you'll see today. Picture where it happens, which room, which person, and walk through that moment once in your mind, doing it. If you pray, you can send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, as Muslims do; if not, simply keep the picture of that one moment.
Khuluq, the Prophet's character and disposition, which Aisha said was simply the Qur'an lived out. Today's word.
Your line: his character was the qur'an. A whole life, learned one habit at a time. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims learn the Prophet's character from the Qur'an and the hadith collections, and many try to copy his everyday habits, such as smiling, helping at home and speaking gently, as part of following his sunnah.

notes: Muslim 746: Sa'd ibn Hisham's questions to Aisha; the exchange is paraphrased and compressed. Confirm framing (he came with several questions; 'at a doorway' is scene-setting only and could be cut).
Pickthall 68:4 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording.
Bukhari 676 (serving his family, going out at prayer time) and Bukhari 6038 (Anas, ten years, never said 'uff'): paraphrased; 'ten years' is stated in that hadith. Confirm numbers.
Tirmidhi 1956 (smiling in your brother's face is charity): confirm number.
